classification.difficultyReason: Draw and extend a triangle, measure the specified angles, and compare their sums with explicitly stated relationships; no theorem discovery or choice of strategy is required.

questions.mappingNote: Part a creates the shared configuration. Part b checks the triangle angle sum through measurements. Part c checks the exterior-angle theorem at B, where AB has been extended beyond B.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 investigates the interior-angle sum by measurement; pages 3–4 establish the interior-angle and exterior-angle theorems; page 5 Examples 1–2 apply those relationships. General protractor measurement instruction is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw and measure a triangle to verify the two directly taught angle relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies the triangle angle sum, sometimes after identifying opposite or alternate angles.

questions.mappingNote: Triangle angle sum is directly requested in every part. Parts e–h additionally use vertically opposite angles; i uses alternate angles. General prerequisite teaching for these angle relationships is absent.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves the triangle angle sum; page 5 Example 1 substitutes known angles into the sum. Pages 3–4 use alternate and corresponding angles in proofs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the triangle angle sum, sometimes after identifying opposite or alternate angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses exterior-angle equations with supplementary or vertically opposite angles.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly requests the exterior-angle theorem. Parts c, d and h solve a sum equation; e–h also need straight-angle or vertically opposite relationships.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 proves the exterior-angle theorem; page 5 Example 2 demonstrates adding opposite interior angles or subtracting a known interior angle from an exterior angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses exterior-angle equations with supplementary or vertically opposite angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Explains possible angle combinations using the triangle angle sum and supplementary exterior angles.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c apply the angle-sum restriction; d–e combine this with supplementary exterior angles. Part e has a material ambiguity because the source explicitly permits two exterior angles at a vertex.
questions.methodNote: The triangle angle sum restricts possible interior angles. Page 3 defines exterior angles as supplementary to adjacent interior angles and explicitly shows two equal exterior angles at one vertex.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explains possible angle combinations using the triangle angle sum and supplementary exterior angles.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest diagrams require selecting connected triangles and transferring an intermediate angle through successive exterior-angle calculations, sometimes using supplementary or vertically opposite angles.

questions.mappingNote: 5a–c combine a straight angle with an exterior angle; 5d–e first recover two interior angles; 5f–g apply the theorem to connected triangles; 5h also uses vertically opposite angles. No parallel-line calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies supplementary straight angles and vertically opposite exterior angles. Page 4 states and proves the exterior angle theorem. Page 5 Example 2 models adding opposite interior angles and subtracting a known interior angle from an exterior angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine exterior-angle reasoning with straight and vertically opposite angles in connected triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the triangle sum or exterior-angle relationship, translate repeated pronumerals into a simple linear equation, and solve; one diagram first requires identifying a vertically opposite angle.

questions.mappingNote: 6a–c and 6g use the triangle angle sum with repeated pronumerals. 6d–e and 6h use the exterior angle theorem. 6f obtains the apex angle using vertically opposite angles, then uses the triangle angle sum.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 establish the triangle angle sum, supplementary straight angles, vertically opposite angles and the exterior angle theorem. Page 5 Examples 1–2 demonstrate forming an angle equation and finding an unknown.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form and solve simple angle equations containing repeated or multiplied pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the relevant marked parallel lines and transversals, then sequence alternate or co-interior angle facts with triangle sums or exterior angles across connected regions.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts combine marked parallel lines with triangle reasoning; finding unknown angles with parallel lines is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle angle-sum theorem and exterior-angle theorem, with named triangles and angle reasons as demonstrated on pages 3–5. Parallel-angle facts appear in the proofs, but their general prerequisite treatment is missing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties with triangle angle sums, exterior angles and straight angles, giving reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Select useful triangles and intermediate angles without labelled unknowns; the hardest cases require establishing parallelism from equal alternate angles or shared perpendiculars before applying further angle relationships.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts combine triangle-angle reasoning with point or parallel-line properties. The closest directly assessed skill is unknown-angles-parallel; parts c and d use triangle sums and exterior angles without a supplied parallel relationship.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves the triangle angle sum and defines exterior angles; page 4 proves the exterior-angle theorem; page 5 Examples 1–2 demonstrate named-triangle equations with reasons. Parallel-angle properties are used in the proofs but their general prerequisite treatment and converses are absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties, triangle angle sums and exterior angles in nine compound diagrams, giving reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify named circle features directly from a labelled diagram.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for a circle feature, so circle-features directly matches the complete assessed task.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of centre, radius and diameter on page 9, chord and major/minor arcs on page 10, and the summary on page 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify named circle features directly from a labelled diagram.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify named circle features and distinguish major and minor arcs in a supplied diagram.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess the circle vocabulary introduced on pages 9–10 and summarised on page 11; circle-features is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of centre, radius, diameter and chord, and identify the larger and smaller curved parts between two points as major and minor arcs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify named circle features and distinguish major and minor arcs in a supplied diagram.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow explicit compass settings and labelling instructions, then check equal intervals using measurement or differences between successive radii.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly applies the taught centre/radius construction and names points and intervals; circle-features is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Set the compass opening to the required radius using a ruler, hold its point at the centre and rotate without changing the opening. Repeat at the same centre for concentric circles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct concentric circles using specified radii, label their intersections with a diameter and check equal intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Maintain a fixed compass radius through a dependent sequence of intersecting circles, then construct an enclosing circle.

questions.mappingNote: Circle features is the closest supplied catalogue skill: the task directly uses centres, equal radii, intersections and an enclosing circle. Geometry notation supports the successive point labels.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches drawing a circle by fixing the compass opening and placing its point at the centre, and establishes the constant radius. Page 10 demonstrates intersecting compass circles. Pages 3 and 5 concern triangle angles and are not needed for this construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Maintain a fixed compass radius through a dependent sequence of intersecting circles, then construct an enclosing circle.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two named side lengths and their included angle into a ruler-and-protractor construction, then measure the remaining side to the requested precision.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing the included 110-degree angle is the most advanced directly assessed skill available in the supplied catalogue; the side lengths and labels are retained as essential construction givens.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 3 models constructing labelled intervals of prescribed lengths with ruler and compasses. The assigned task instead supplies an included angle and requires protractor construction followed by ruler measurement. The inspected pages do not teach that prerequisite protractor method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle from two side lengths and their included obtuse angle, then measure the remaining side.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a specified base and two angle rays on the same side to locate their intersection, then apply the triangle sum and measure the remaining sides.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed construction uses an included side and two angles. Part b applies the triangle angle sum; part c measures the same construction. Protractor construction is the closest available primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves the triangle angle sum; page 5 applies it by subtracting known angles. Pages 9–10 introduce compasses and triangle construction from three side lengths. They do not teach the protractor construction required here or ruler measurement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle from a side and two angles, explain its third angle and measure the remaining sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify named features of an isosceles triangle, measure its legs and base angles, and state the equal-base-angle property.

questions.mappingNote: Classifying and naming isosceles-triangle features is the main assessed skill; angle measurement and notation are secondary. Original prerequisite ruler/protractor instruction is absent from the supplied evidence.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 define legs, apex, base and base angles and state equality of base angles. Page 15 requests protractor confirmation but does not teach protractor placement or scale reading. Pages 3–4 and Example 6 on page 16 supply angle-theorem context; this question requires direct measurement rather than angle-sum calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify named features of an isosceles triangle, measure its legs and base angles, and state the equal-base-angle property.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate missing interior angles, including from exterior angles, and test for two equal angles.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly asks for classification using equal angles. Parts b–d and f require interior-angle calculations; part e uses the exterior-angle theorem. No protractor or general parallel-line prerequisite is needed.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 give the equal-angle test for isosceles triangles; page 3 supplies the triangle angle sum and supplementary interior/exterior angles; page 4 supplies the exterior-angle theorem. Pages 15–16 model concise angle calculations with geometric reasons.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate missing interior angles, including from exterior angles, and test for two equal angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Draw the described figures, recognise equal sides or radii, and combine equal base angles with straight-angle or triangle-angle sums.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines a straight angle at C with equal base angles opposite AB and AC. Part b follows Example 4 directly using equal radii and the triangle angle sum. Neither part requires the missing general parallel-line prerequisite treatment.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 establish equal base angles and equal radii forming an isosceles triangle. Page 15 Example 4 subtracts the central angle from 180 degrees and halves the remainder. Page 16 Example 6 uses a straight angle with an exterior angle; pages 3–4 supply triangle angle-sum and exterior-angle context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw the described figures, recognise equal sides or radii, and combine equal base angles with straight-angle or triangle-angle sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a 60° angle by applying the taught equilateral-triangle construction with equal-radius compass arcs.

questions.mappingNote: The closest available catalogue skill is angle construction, although its title specifies a protractor. This question requires compasses and a straight edge; the equilateral-triangle property supplies the justification.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 teaches constructing 60° at an interval endpoint using intersecting arcs of the same radius and the equal angles of an equilateral triangle. Pages 18 and 20 provide the surrounding compass-and-straight-edge construction context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a 60° angle by applying the taught equilateral-triangle construction with equal-radius compass arcs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught straight-angle bisection construction at an endpoint, with the initial extension explicitly supplied. Sloping and vertical orientations require the same construction.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly applies this construction to sloping and vertical intervals. The closest supplied skill is perpendicular-lines; no compass-construction skill is present in the supplied catalogue.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 constructs an endpoint right angle by extending the interval and bisecting the resulting straight angle. Its second pair of equal-radius arcs has a larger radius than the first arc.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the straight-angle bisection construction in two orientations using compasses and a straight edge.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a taught 60-degree or right-angle construction, bisect as needed, and recognise that 150 and 135 degrees can be obtained by taking supplements of constructed angles.

questions.mappingNote: The question combines precisely these constructions. Parts c and d take supplements of the constructed 30-degree and 45-degree angles, as confirmed by the teacher answers. The available construction skill names a protractor; it is the closest taxonomy match, but no protractor is permitted here.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 demonstrates angle bisection and constructing a right angle by bisecting a straight angle. Page 19 demonstrates the equilateral-triangle construction of 60 degrees and successive bisection to obtain 30, 15, 45 and 22½ degrees. Page 20 requires compass-and-straight-edge constructions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine equilateral-triangle, right-angle and angle-bisection constructions; use supplementary angles in parts c and d. The closest catalogue skill concerns angle construction, although this task uses compasses and a straight edge.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the equal-radius compass-arc construction to three different intervals.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses a compass-and-straight-edge perpendicular-bisector construction. The supplied catalogue has no dedicated construction skill; perpendicular-lines is the closest existing skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 demonstrates the perpendicular bisector: draw equal-radius arcs from the two endpoints, then join their two intersections. Symmetry establishes perpendicularity and bisection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the equal-radius compass-arc construction to three different intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the named, taught perpendicular-dropping construction from an external point. Choosing three intervals changes the drawings but introduces no new construction strategy.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly applies dropping a perpendicular. The catalogue has no compass-construction skill; perpendicular-lines is the closest directly assessed relationship.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 demonstrates an arc centred at an external point, equal-radius arcs from its two intersections with the given line, and the perpendicular through the external point and the second arc intersection. Pages 18–19 establish equal radii and perpendicular-bisector constructions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated perpendicular construction to three independently drawn intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise repeated bisections into halves, quarters and eighths, and construct adjacent angle bisectors to check perpendicularity. The requested outcomes guide both construction sequences.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess compass-and-straight-edge angle construction. The nearest available construction taxonomy item names a protractor; no protractor method is substituted. Part a additionally uses supplementary angles and perpendicularity.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 teaches angle bisection using an arc centred at the vertex and equal-radius intersecting arcs from its intersections with the arms. Page 19 applies repeated bisection to construct further angles. Page 20 establishes Exercise 13D and compass-and-straight-edge construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine repeated angle bisection with a check that bisectors of supplementary angles are perpendicular. The closest construction skill names a protractor, but these tasks require compasses and a straight edge.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine perpendicular constructions and compass transfer of equal lengths to construct a square.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task combines square properties with perpendicular construction. The catalogue has no compass-and-straight-edge construction skill; quadrilateral-properties is the closest available match.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 constructs a perpendicular at an interval endpoint by bisecting a straight angle and explains equal circle radii. Pages 19–20 reinforce equal-radius compass constructions. Apply endpoint perpendiculars twice and transfer the chosen side length using compasses.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine perpendicular constructions and compass transfer of equal lengths to construct a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise perpendicular diameters as a way to locate an inscribed square, then use the prescribed central-angle bisections and extend them to obtain eight equally spaced points.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied catalogue has no compass-construction skill. Quadrilateral properties is the closest primary match because the task constructs an inscribed square using its perpendicular equal diagonals; perpendicular lines and circle features support the construction.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 teaches equal-radius compass-arc angle bisection and perpendicular construction. Page 19 teaches perpendicular bisectors and repeated angle bisection. Page 20 establishes the compass-and-straight-edge exercise context. Apply those constructions to perpendicular diameters, then bisect adjacent central right angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine perpendicular-diameter and angle-bisection constructions to inscribe a square and locate eight equally spaced points.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate each missing angle and realise the angle set in a drawing. The three 10-degree angles force a 330-degree reflex interior angle, requiring a non-convex figure and careful distinction between its interior and notch angles.

questions.mappingNote: Each part combines quadrilateral angle-sum calculation with an angle-controlled drawing. Part e requires a reflex interior angle.
questions.methodNote: Subtract the three supplied angles from 360°. The source defines non-convex quadrilaterals and their reflex angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a missing angle and draw an example, including a non-convex quadrilateral.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine quadrilateral angle sums, parallel-line relationships and an exterior angle.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines parallel sides and a right angle; b uses two equal unknowns in the angle sum; c uses both marked pairs of parallel sides; d finds an exterior angle after finding the interior angle.
questions.methodNote: Use the quadrilateral angle sum and straight angles. Parts a and c additionally require supplementary co-interior angles on parallel lines; the supplied pages use parallel-line properties in proofs but do not supply the general prerequisite treatment.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine quadrilateral angle sums, parallel-line relationships and an exterior angle.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest part requires finding a total angle without knowing either component: recognise two isosceles triangles, represent their unknown vertex-angle split, and combine their base-angle expressions using the supplied right angle.

questions.mappingNote: 5a uses the two equal-sided triangles around D; 5b splits the right angle between two isosceles triangles; 5c converts supplementary angles before using the outer isosceles triangle; 5d uses common perpendiculars and co-interior angles; 5e applies the quadrilateral sum; 5f uses a triangle sum followed by a quadrilateral sum.
questions.methodNote: Use triangle and quadrilateral angle sums, straight and full angles, and equal base angles. Parallel and perpendicular prerequisites needed by 5d are not fully taught in the supplied context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires several linked deductions using equal sides, auxiliary segments and angle sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the floor plan to identify the shelf's right angle, derive its equal base angles, and transfer the sloping-wall angle between parallel room boundaries before finding the table's supplementary vertex angle and equal base angles.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts combine isosceles-triangle properties with angles inferred from the floor plan, making unknown-sides-angles-figures the closest assessed skill. Pages 22–23 establish the exercise context. Page 9 supplies no additional method needed here.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes the triangle angle sum and supplementary angles on a straight line. Page 13 states equal base angles in an isosceles triangle; page 15 Example 4 subtracts the known angle from 180 degrees and halves the remainder. Part b additionally requires parallel-line angle properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer angles in two isosceles triangles using a shared floor plan, perpendicular boundaries and a straight outer wall.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties with vertically opposite angles, triangle angle sums and an auxiliary parallel line.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d primarily assess unknown angles with parallel lines; part a additionally uses vertically opposite angles and the triangle angle sum. The attached pages use parallel-line facts but do not supply the general prerequisite treatment required for complete taught-method reconciliation.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 proves the triangle angle sum using alternate angles on a parallel line; page 4 constructs a parallel ray and adds adjacent angles in the exterior-angle proof. Page 5 demonstrates triangle-angle calculations with reasons. Page 22 teaches the quadrilateral angle sum. Apply corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle properties, adding a parallel ray through M in part d.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties with vertically opposite angles, triangle angle sums and an auxiliary parallel line.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine triangle angle sums, exterior angles and parallel-line relationships; solve simple equations involving multiples of unknown angles.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the exterior-angle theorem directly; b combines the triangle sum with vertically opposite angles; c solves the triangle-sum equation; d subtracts the right angle from an exterior angle; e uses corresponding angles then the triangle sum; f solves the exterior-angle equation. No offered reuse candidate is the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–5 establish the triangle angle sum and exterior-angle theorem, with reasoned angle equations. Page 22 concerns quadrilateral angle sums and supplies no additional method needed here. Parts b and e also require prerequisite angle-pair facts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine triangle angle sums, exterior angles and parallel-line relationships; solve simple equations involving multiples of unknown angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine equal radii, isosceles base angles, parallel-line angles and triangle or quadrilateral angle sums.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 9 and 13 establish equal radii and isosceles base angles; page 15 Example 4 directly models c. Page 22 models quadrilateral angle sums. Pages 3–4 demonstrate alternate-angle reasoning, but the original general prerequisite treatment needed for d and f is absent.
questions.methodNote: Equal radii establish isosceles triangles; equal base angles and the triangle angle sum solve a–d. The quadrilateral angle sum solves e and, with vertically opposite angles, f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine equal radii, isosceles base angles, parallel-line angles and triangle or quadrilateral angle sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Use equal angles to establish equal opposite sides after finding angles using exterior-angle or parallel-line properties.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c all assess unknown side lengths through equal angles; part b first derives an angle using the exterior-angle theorem, and part c first derives an angle from parallel lines. The general prerequisite treatment of alternate angles is absent from supplied evidence.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 states that equal angles imply equal opposite sides; page 15 Example 5 applies that test to an unknown length. Page 4 supplies the exterior-angle theorem used in part b. Part c uses alternate angles, as used in the proofs on pages 3–4, then triangle angle sum and equal opposite sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use equal angles to establish equal opposite sides after finding angles using exterior-angle or parallel-line properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct triangles from three side lengths and from two equal legs with a specified included angle.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly adapts the page 10 three-side construction. Part b combines the page 13 equal-radii construction with a 110-degree protractor construction. The closest available primary skill is construct-angles-protractor; the catalogue has no dedicated three-side triangle-construction skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 3 constructs a triangle from three side lengths using two intersecting circles. Page 13 constructs an isosceles triangle from two radii of a circle, with the centre as apex. Pages 18–20 teach compass constructions but do not supply the missing general protractor procedure.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct triangles from three side lengths and from two equal legs with a specified included angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct an equilateral triangle using equal-radius compass arcs and the equal-side property.

questions.mappingNote: Use the same equal-radius construction with a measured 5 cm base, then join both endpoints to the arc intersection. The closest supplied taxonomy skill is classify-triangles, using the defining equal-side property.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 establishes equality of circle radii. Page 19 constructs an equilateral triangle using intersecting arcs of equal radius to obtain a 60-degree angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an equilateral triangle using equal-radius compass arcs and the equal-side property.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the taught equilateral-triangle and right-angle constructions, then apply successive angle bisections to obtain the requested sizes. Additional bisections repeat the same method rather than require a new connection.

questions.mappingNote: All six responses directly combine these constructions. The closest supplied catalogue skill is construct-angles-protractor, although the source explicitly requires ruler and compasses rather than a protractor.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 teaches compass angle bisection and constructing a right angle by bisecting a straight angle. Page 19 teaches the equilateral-triangle 60° construction and explicitly obtains 30°, 15°, 45° and 22½° by successive bisection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the equilateral-triangle and right-angle constructions with repeated angle bisection, using ruler and compasses.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three compass angle-bisection constructions and a perpendicular construction to locate and draw a circle touching all three sides. The catalogue has no compass-construction skill.

questions.mappingNote: The construction combines the source's elementary compass methods. Equal distances from the arms of each angle follow from the taught folding symmetry; this establishes why the chosen radius works for all three sides without invoking advanced circle theorems. The closest catalogue skill concerns angle construction, although its protractor-specific definition does not cover this compass task exactly.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 teaches angle bisection using one vertex-centred arc followed by equal-radius intersecting arcs, with a folding justification. Page 19 reinforces bisection and perpendicular-bisector construction. Page 20 teaches dropping a perpendicular from a point to a line. Apply those constructions to the same triangle; use the perpendicular distance as the circle radius.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three compass angle-bisection constructions and a perpendicular construction to locate and draw a circle touching all three sides. The catalogue has no compass-construction skill.

classification.difficultyReason: The steps specify constructing each perpendicular bisector and using their intersection as the circle centre; the student applies taught constructions and sets the radius to a vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the page 19 construction separately to all three triangle sides, then use the common point as the circle centre. The equal-distance explanation establishes the intended combination without advanced circle-angle theorems. No standalone triangle-circumcentre procedure is supplied.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 teaches constructing a perpendicular bisector using equal-radius intersecting arcs from the endpoints. Page 18 states that all radii of a circle are equal. Page 20 supplies related compass-and-straight-edge constructions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three perpendicular-bisector constructions and use their common point to construct a circle through the triangle's vertices; the catalogue has no specific compass-construction skill.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest configuration requires introducing auxiliary parallel lines at successive bends, transferring angles and deciding which angles to subtract to obtain the final angle.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f combine parallel-angle reasoning with straight angles or triangle geometry; g–h apply quadrilateral angle sums. General prerequisite teaching for parallel-angle facts is missing from the supplied evidence and remains a content-review dependency.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 apply alternate and corresponding angles with auxiliary parallel lines and establish triangle interior/exterior angle results. Page 22 proves the quadrilateral interior-angle sum and demonstrates subtracting known angles from 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties, straight angles and polygon angle sums across eight figures.

classification.difficultyReason: The construction and both inequality targets are supplied. The student links exterior and isosceles angle facts, interprets a proper angle part, and explains why the contradiction excludes unequal sides in either order.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded stem introduces proof by contradiction. Pages 3–4 provide triangle angle reasoning and the exterior-angle theorem; pages 13–14 provide the isosceles base-angle theorem and identify its converse as the challenge proof.
questions.methodNote: Use the exterior-angle theorem in BCD, equal base angles in ADC, and the strict inequality between a proper angle part and the whole angle. Contradict the assumed inequality of opposite sides.
